info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 9.1: Manual Morphological Parsing, Lemmatization, and Treebanking.

name.text: 01 Question: What Lemmatization and Parsing Accomplish

questiontext.text: Why does digital textual scholarship require morphological parsing and lemmatization rather than relying exclusively on orthographic string matching?

generalfeedback.text: Lemmatization and morphological parsing convert unstructured character sequences into semantically and grammatically queryable linguistic data.

answer.text: String matching cannot bridge inflected surface forms to underlying dictionary headwords or expose the grammatical relationships governing words.

feedback.text: Correct. Raw character matching leaves inflectional paradigms and syntactic government opaque; parsing and lemmatization structure text into queryable linguistic data.

answer.text: String matching is too computationally expensive for modern computers to execute across large historical corpora.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Exact string matching is computationally trivial; the problem is its analytical opacity to inflectional morphology and syntax.

answer.text: Optical character recognition software cannot output raw text strings without first performing lemmatization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. OCR produces raw character streams; lemmatization is a downstream analytical process applied to transcribed text.

answer.text: Digital editions are prohibited by TEI guidelines from storing unparsed orthographic character sequences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI easily accommodates unparsed text; linguistic annotation is an analytical enrichment, not a format requirement.

name.text: 02 Question: The Anatomy of an Inflected Word Form

questiontext.text: What distinguishes the morphology of synthetic, fusional languages like Ancient Greek and Latin from agglutinative languages?

generalfeedback.text: Fusional morphology bundles multiple grammatical categories into single affixes, requiring editors to systematically isolate stems, affixes, and inflectional terminations.

answer.text: Fusional languages compress multiple grammatical categories into single, indivisible affixes rather than stringing together discrete, one-to-one morphemes.

feedback.text: Correct. In fusional languages, a single affix simultaneously encodes multiple categories (e.g. Greek -ων encoding genitive, plural, and gender) rather than isolated single-feature affixes.

answer.text: Fusional languages rely entirely on periphrastic auxiliary verbs rather than attaching inflectional affixes to stems.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Analytic languages use periphrastic auxiliaries; fusional languages attach synthetic affixes to stems.

answer.text: Agglutinative languages fuse lexical roots and stems so thoroughly that morpheme boundaries cannot be distinguished.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Agglutinative languages maintain clean, segmented, one-to-one morpheme boundaries; fusional languages compress multiple features into single affixes.

answer.text: Fusional languages never modify the lexical root through temporal augments, reduplication, or ablaut.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fusional languages routinely alter lexical roots via augments, reduplication, and ablaut vowel gradation.

name.text: 03 Question: The Concept of the Lemma and Lexicographical Conventions

questiontext.text: Why must an annotator strictly follow a specific language tradition's canonical citation convention when assigning a lemma?

generalfeedback.text: A lemma is a standardized lexicographical citation form, and manual annotation must strictly follow the reference authority's canonical convention.

answer.text: A lemma is a standardized lexicographical citation convention, and diverging from canonical standards breaks interoperability with downstream databases.

feedback.text: Correct. Lexicographical traditions establish specific citation forms (e.g. LSJ first-person singular present active for Greek verbs); using non-standard forms disrupts computational linking.

answer.text: Universal linguistic principles dictate that the infinitive form must always be the lemma in every human language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Citation conventions vary by language family: Greek/Latin use first-person present active indicative, Semitic languages use third-person masculine perfect roots, and modern Romance languages use infinitives.

answer.text: Lemmas are physical entities discovered directly inside manuscript witnesses rather than editorial conventions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A lemma is an abstract editorial convention chosen to represent an entire inflectional paradigm in dictionaries.

answer.text: Downstream treebanks and NLP parsers automatically convert arbitrary citation forms into valid identifiers without errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NLP pipelines and alignment databases rely on exact string matches against canonical dictionary headwords.

name.text: 04 Question: Tokenization and Segmental Ambiguity

questiontext.text: Why is tokenization in historical manuscript editing considered an interpretive philological act rather than a mechanical string split?

generalfeedback.text: Tokenization is an interpretive philological decision that requires isolating enclitics, crasis, and contracted forms into discrete grammatical units.

answer.text: Manuscript continuous script, enclitics, crasis, and elision require editors to decide where discrete grammatical words begin and end.

feedback.text: Correct. Scribes wrote in scriptio continua or used contracted forms like crasis (κἀγώ) and enclitics (-que), requiring grammatical interpretation to establish token boundaries.

answer.text: Modern Unicode standards require all ancient texts to be tokenized into fixed three-letter segments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tokenization establishes linguistic word boundaries, not arbitrary character-length chunks.

answer.text: Tokenization requires determining the font family and ink composition used by the historical scribe.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font and ink analysis belong to paleography/codicology, not grammatical token segmentation.

answer.text: Punctuation in medieval manuscripts always marks exact sentence and clause boundaries identical to modern syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscript punctuation is idiosyncratic and rarely aligns systematically with modern syntactic clause boundaries.

name.text: 05 Question: Morphological Ambiguity and Paradigmatic Syncretism

questiontext.text: How does a human philologist resolve paradigmatic syncretism during manual morphological parsing?

generalfeedback.text: Paradigmatic syncretism creates pervasive surface ambiguity that can only be resolved through systematic analysis of syntactic context and semantic government.

answer.text: By analyzing the surrounding syntactic context, verbal case government, agreement markers, and discourse semantics.

feedback.text: Correct. Paradigmatic syncretism creates surface homophony; the correct analysis can only be identified by synthesizing syntactic government and semantic context.

answer.text: By selecting the shortest dictionary definition listed in the reference lexicon.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Definition length has no bearing on grammatical case, number, or part-of-speech selection.

answer.text: By defaulting to nominative singular masculine whenever a noun form is ambiguous.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Defaulting to an arbitrary baseline corrupts morphological distributions and distorts syntactic analysis.

answer.text: By removing ambiguous tokens from the digital edition's text stream entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editions preserve all attested text and resolve ambiguous morphology in context.

name.text: 06 Question: Verbal Complexity: Stems, Aspect, and Principal Parts

questiontext.text: Why cannot Ancient Greek verb forms be parsed accurately through simple, naive suffix stripping?

generalfeedback.text: Ancient verbal systems rely on distinct aspectual stems and suppletive roots, requiring philological identification of principal parts rather than naive affix stripping.

answer.text: Greek verbs construct aspectual stems through deep phonological changes, ablaut, reduplication, and suppletive roots across six principal parts.

feedback.text: Correct. Greek verbal morphology relies on distinct aspectual stems and suppletive roots (e.g. ὁράω, ὄψομαι, εἶδον) that cannot be derived by stripping suffixes from a single base.

answer.text: Ancient Greek verbs lack inflectional suffixes entirely, relying exclusively on independent preverbal particles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek verbs are heavily inflected with synthetic personal and mood suffixes attached to aspectual stems.

answer.text: Greek verbs inflect identically across all conjugations without any irregular or athematic paradigms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Greek possesses complex thematic and athematic (mi-verb) conjugations with widespread irregular paradigms.

answer.text: Suffix stripping is prohibited by international copyright restrictions on Greek lexicographical databases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Suffix stripping fails due to linguistic and phonological reality, not legal or copyright restrictions.

name.text: 07 Question: Nominal and Adjectival Inflection: Agreement and Case Government

questiontext.text: In Classical Greek and Latin nominal parsing, what principle ensures grammatical agreement between a substantive and an attributive adjective?

generalfeedback.text: Nominal parsing involves identifying declension classes, verifying gender-number-case agreement across phrases, and establishing syntactic case government.

answer.text: They must share identical gender, number, and case, even if they belong to different declension classes and carry different surface endings.

feedback.text: Correct. Agreement is syntactic and feature-based: a third-declension noun and first-declension adjective agree in gender, number, and case despite having distinct inflectional terminations.

answer.text: They must share identical character lengths and phonological vowel quantities in their terminations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Agreement depends on grammatical feature concordance (gender/number/case), not syllable length or phonological identity.

answer.text: They must both belong to the exact same declension class and stem paradigm.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives routinely modify substantives of different declension classes (e.g. first-declension adjective modifying a third-declension noun).

answer.text: Adjectives in classical languages do not inflect for case and remain indeclinable modifiers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjectives in Greek and Latin inflect fully for case, number, and gender to agree with their governing nouns.

name.text: 08 Question: Closed-Class Categories: Particles, Conjunctions, and Prepositions

questiontext.text: Why does manual parsing of historical closed-class words like Greek prepositions and particles require syntactic analysis?

generalfeedback.text: Closed-class particles and prepositions must be categorized by their specific syntactic function and case government rather than treated as static lexical glosses.

answer.text: Many closed-class tokens are polysemous homographs whose function and meaning depend on the specific case they govern or the discourse clause they modulate.

feedback.text: Correct. A single preposition like παρά changes meaning completely depending on whether it governs genitive, dative, or accusative, while particles modulate modal semantics.

answer.text: Closed-class words constantly undergo unpredictable nominal declension across all nine morphological cases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Closed-class functional words are indeclinable; their complexity lies in polysemy, homography, and case government.

answer.text: Prepositions in Ancient Greek and Latin always govern only the nominative case.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prepositions govern oblique cases (genitive, dative, accusative, ablative), never the nominative.

answer.text: Particles were added exclusively by nineteenth-century typographers and do not represent historical language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Discourse particles are integral elements of ancient Greek narrative and philosophical prose.

name.text: 09 Question: The Universal Dependencies Taxonomy and UPOS Tagset

questiontext.text: What is the structural role of the 17 Universal Part-of-Speech (UPOS) tags in the Universal Dependencies framework?

generalfeedback.text: The Universal Dependencies UPOS tagset provides 17 standardized, cross-linguistic categories that establish the foundational part-of-speech classification for every token.

answer.text: They provide a standardized, coarse-grained, cross-linguistically consistent part-of-speech taxonomy applicable to every human language.

feedback.text: Correct. The 17 UPOS tags establish a fixed, universal classification ensuring that core grammatical categories are comparable across languages and corpora.

answer.text: They replace all language-specific grammatical descriptions with a single numeric ranking from 1 to 17.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UPOS tags are standardized categorical labels (e.g. NOUN, VERB, ADJ), not numeric quality rankings.

answer.text: They provide fine-grained inflectional case and mood details for Greek dialectal poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coarse UPOS tags provide high-level parts of speech; detailed inflectional features are stored in FEATS and XPOS.

answer.text: They are proprietary tags licensed exclusively to commercial natural language processing platforms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Universal Dependencies is an open, international academic standard developed for cross-linguistic research.

name.text: 10 Question: Language-Specific Part-of-Speech Tags and Positional Tagsets

questiontext.text: How is morphological information encoded in the Perseus 9-position XPOS positional tagset?

generalfeedback.text: Positional XPOS tagsets use a 9-character code to record the complete inflectional profile of a historical word form in a standardized, machine-readable syntax.

answer.text: As a fixed-length 9-character string where each specific position maps deterministically to a morphological dimension, with hyphens marking non-applicable features.

feedback.text: Correct. The 9-position code dedicates positions to POS, person, number, tense, mood, voice, gender, case, and degree (e.g. v3sria---), using hyphens for inapplicable slots.

answer.text: As a comma-separated list of English grammatical definitions enclosed in brackets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Positional XPOS uses a compact 9-character positional string, not free English prose.

answer.text: As a variable-length binary bitmask encoding Unicode character offsets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Perseus tagset uses readable single-letter codes in a fixed 9-character layout.

answer.text: As an unstructured XML comment placed at the end of the document body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Positional tags are structured machine-readable strings stored directly in token metadata.

name.text: 11 Question: Morphosyntactic Features in Universal Dependencies

questiontext.text: How does the Universal Dependencies FEATS standard structure morphological properties?

generalfeedback.text: The Universal Dependencies FEATS standard encodes morphological properties as sorted, pipe-delimited key-value pairs for transparent data exchange.

answer.text: As an alphabetically sorted, pipe-delimited list of explicit key-value pairs without spaces around equals signs.

feedback.text: Correct. The FEATS column formats features as explicit key-value pairs (e.g. Case=Nom|Gender=Masc|Number=Sing) sorted alphabetically for transparent data exchange.

answer.text: As a single 9-digit floating-point number representing grammatical probability.

feedback.text: Incorrect. FEATS uses structured key-value strings, not probabilistic numerical values.

answer.text: As an unorganized paragraph of Latin prose describing the word's etymology.

feedback.text: Incorrect. FEATS specifies structured, machine-actionable morphological features, not etymological prose.

answer.text: As an encrypted binary blob readable only by dedicated proprietary hardware.

feedback.text: Incorrect. FEATS strings are standard UTF-8 plain text designed for open interoperability.

name.text: 12 Question: Principles of Dependency Grammar for Historical Languages

questiontext.text: Why is dependency grammar superior to phrase-structure constituency grammar for modeling ancient Greek and Latin syntax?

generalfeedback.text: Dependency grammar models direct head-dependent relations between words, providing a robust syntax model for the flexible word order and hyperbaton of ancient languages.

answer.text: Dependency grammar models direct head-dependent relations between words, making it invariant under free word order, discontinuous constituents, and hyperbaton.

feedback.text: Correct. Because dependency links connect words directly rather than through rigid nested phrase boxes, the syntax model remains robust under word-order permutations and hyperbaton.

answer.text: Constituency grammar cannot represent sentences containing more than five words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Constituency grammar can model long sentences, but it struggles with non-projective word order and discontinuous constituents in inflected languages.

answer.text: Dependency grammar requires all verbs to be placed strictly at the end of the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dependency grammar makes no assumptions about word order; links connect semantic heads and dependents regardless of linear position.

answer.text: Classical languages were written without grammar rules, making phrase structures impossible to formulate.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Classical languages possessed rich, rigorous grammatical systems; dependency grammar simply models their non-configurational syntax more effectively.

name.text: 13 Question: Syntactic Dependency Relations in Universal Dependencies

questiontext.text: In the Universal Dependencies DEPREL framework, what structural principle governs prepositional phrases such as ἐν τῇ πόλει?

generalfeedback.text: Universal Dependencies DEPREL tags specify the exact grammatical relation connecting each dependent word to its governing semantic head.

answer.text: Content words are privileged as heads: the noun (πόλει) is the head of the phrase, while the preposition (ἐν) attaches to it with the relation 'case'.

feedback.text: Correct. In modern UD, content words act as heads: the preposition attaches as a 'case' dependent and the article as 'det' to the noun head.

answer.text: The preposition is always the root head of the entire sentence, governing all verbs and nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The main finite verb is typically the sentence root; prepositions attach to their nominal complements.

answer.text: The article is treated as the head governing both the preposition and the noun.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Articles attach to nouns with the 'det' relation; they never serve as heads of content nouns in UD.

answer.text: Prepositions and articles are deleted from the dependency tree because they carry no grammatical meaning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every token in the sentence is integrated into the dependency tree with specific relations like 'case' and 'det'.

name.text: 14 Question: The Ancient Greek and Latin Dependency Treebank Standard

questiontext.text: What is the primary structural difference between the legacy AGLDT Prague-style treebank schema and the modern Universal Dependencies standard?

generalfeedback.text: The AGLDT standard provided the historical foundation for classical treebanking, which has now been harmonized into the content-head architecture of Universal Dependencies.

answer.text: Legacy AGLDT treated function words (like prepositions and auxiliaries) as heads governing content words, whereas modern UD treats content words as heads.

feedback.text: Correct. Legacy Prague/AGLDT placed prepositions (AuxP) as heads governing nouns; UD inverted this to establish content words as heads with function words as dependents.

answer.text: Legacy AGLDT banned the annotation of Latin texts, focusing exclusively on Attic oratory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AGLDT included extensive Latin corpora (Cicero, Caesar, Virgil, Jerome) as well as Greek.

answer.text: Modern UD forbids the inclusion of morphological feature tags on word tokens.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern UD fully supports and standardizes morphological features via UPOS, XPOS, and FEATS.

answer.text: Legacy AGLDT was encoded in proprietary binary formats that could not be converted to plain text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AGLDT was encoded in XML and has been successfully mapped to Universal Dependencies format.

name.text: 15 Question: The PROIEL Treebank Architecture and Biblical Corpora

questiontext.text: What theoretical innovation did the PROIEL treebank project introduce to historical dependency annotation?

generalfeedback.text: The PROIEL treebank provides an expertly annotated, gold-standard reference for biblical and historical corpora, pioneering the integration of syntax, pragmatics, and secondary predication.

answer.text: It integrated syntactic dependency trees with pragmatic information packaging, discourse referentiality, and dual-index secondary predication.

feedback.text: Correct. PROIEL advanced historical treebanking by modeling syntax alongside information structure (topic/focus), anaphora, and secondary predication (e.g. participles).

answer.text: It eliminated manual annotation entirely, relying on unverified automated neural parsers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PROIEL was manually annotated and verified by expert philologists, creating a gold-standard reference.

answer.text: It restricted its corpus strictly to modern twentieth-century vernacular translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PROIEL focused on ancient Indo-European biblical translations in Greek, Latin, Gothic, Classical Armenian, and Old Church Slavonic.

answer.text: It replaced dependency trees with flat, unannotated character word lists.

feedback.text: Incorrect. PROIEL created rich, multi-layered syntactic and pragmatic dependency graphs.

name.text: 16 Question: Manual Annotation Protocols and Scholarly Lexica

questiontext.text: What is the purpose of establishing an explicit four-step verification protocol during manual parsing?

generalfeedback.text: A standardized four-step manual protocol backed by authoritative lexica guarantees that gold-standard annotations remain methodologically sound and consistent.

answer.text: To guarantee that surface identification, lexical lookup, morphological decomposition, and syntactic attachment remain internally consistent and methodologically sound.

feedback.text: Correct. A standardized four-step protocol backed by authoritative lexica ensures that ground-truth annotations are rigorous, reproducible, and documented across all tokens.

answer.text: To ensure that manual annotations can be completed in less than five seconds per paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual parsing prioritizes philological rigor and accuracy over rapid processing speed.

answer.text: To prevent human editors from consulting scholarly dictionaries like LSJ or Lewis and Short.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The protocol explicitly requires querying authoritative lexica (LSJ, OLD, ThLL) for verification.

answer.text: To automatically generate XML files without requiring any editorial review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The protocol defines disciplined human editorial review to produce the reference ground truth.

name.text: 17 Question: TEI P5 Chapter 18: Simple Analytic Mechanisms

questiontext.text: What is the main architectural advantage of TEI P5 Chapter 18's inline linguistic segmentation over ISO Feature Structures?

generalfeedback.text: TEI P5 Chapter 18 defines lightweight inline XML mechanisms that embed morphological analysis directly into the text stream of a digital edition.

answer.text: It embeds analytical attributes directly on word () and punctuation () elements in the text stream, avoiding verbose and complex standoff XML structures.

feedback.text: Correct. Chapter 18 provides a lightweight inline mechanism that attaches lemma, POS, and morphosyntactic descriptions directly to text tokens in and tags.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for XML validation schemas, allowing arbitrary tag syntax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Chapter 18 conforms strictly to TEI P5 XML schemas and validation rules.

answer.text: It separates the diplomatic transcription into an encrypted external database.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Chapter 18 keeps the diplomatic text inline while enriching it with analytical XML attributes.

answer.text: It forces all digital editions to be published exclusively in printed book format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI Chapter 18 is designed specifically for computational processing and digital edition interfaces.

name.text: 18 Question: The att.linguistic Attribute Class in TEI XML

questiontext.text: Which group of attributes is provided by the TEI att.linguistic attribute class on the element?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI att.linguistic attribute class provides standardized @lemma, @pos, and @msd attributes to store morphological analyses directly on elements.

answer.text: @lemma, @lemmaRef, @pos, @msd, and @join.

feedback.text: Correct. The att.linguistic class provides @lemma (headword), @lemmaRef (lexicon URI), @pos (part of speech), @msd (morphosyntactic description), and @join (clitic attachment).

answer.text: @src, @href, @alt, and @target.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are generic linking and media attributes, not the linguistic class attributes defined in Chapter 18.

answer.text: @meter, @rhyme, @stanza, and @caesura.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These attributes belong to verse and metrical analysis modules, not att.linguistic.

answer.text: @wit, @rdg, @lem, and @app.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These belong to the Chapter 13 textcrit module for apparatus encoding, not linguistic analysis.

name.text: 19 Question: Segmenting Sentences, Words, and Punctuation in TEI XML

questiontext.text: How are sentences, words, and punctuation structured in a fully compliant TEI Chapter 18 document?

generalfeedback.text: Full TEI linguistic encoding wraps sentences in , words in , and punctuation in , assigning unique @xml:id anchors to every token.

answer.text: Sentences are wrapped in , words in , and punctuation marks in , each carrying a unique @xml:id anchor.

feedback.text: Correct. The structural hierarchy wraps clauses/sentences in , lexical words in , and punctuation in , assigning unique @xml:id attributes for downstream linking.

answer.text:
All tokens are merged into a single unstructured

element without individual word tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Full linguistic tokenization requires explicit segmentation into , , and elements.

answer.text: Punctuation marks must be deleted from the XML file to prevent parsing errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation characters are preserved and classified inside elements.

answer.text: Every letter in the sentence must be enclosed in an independent tag with font descriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character-level tags are used only for specialized graphemic studies, not standard linguistic tokenization.

name.text: 20 Question: Step-by-Step Manual Parsing Walkthrough: Classical Greek Prose

questiontext.text: In the manual parse of Plato's Apology 17a (Ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς ... πεπόνθατε ... οὐκ οἶδα), what is the syntactic root and how does πεπόνθατε attach to it?

generalfeedback.text: Manual parsing systematically resolves every token's lemma, morphosyntactic feature bundle, and syntactic dependency attachment within the sentence hierarchy.

answer.text: The matrix verb οἶδα is the root (HEAD=0, DEPREL=root), and πεπόνθατε attaches to it as a clausal complement (DEPREL=ccomp).

feedback.text: Correct. The main finite clause is headed by οἶδα ('I do not know'), and the subordinate clause headed by πεπόνθατε ('what you have experienced') functions as its clausal complement.

answer.text: The interjection ὦ is the root, and all other words attach as vocatives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Interjections and vocatives are peripheral discourse elements, not the structural root of the clause.

answer.text: The pronoun ὑμεῖς is the root, and οἶδα is an adjectival modifier.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Nominal subjects depend on their governing verbs; a pronoun cannot be the clausal root over a finite verb.

answer.text: The preposition ὑπὸ is the root, governing the entire sentence as an adverbial phrase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prepositions attach to their nominal complements; they do not serve as matrix roots of complex sentences.

name.text: 21 Question: Step-by-Step Manual Parsing Walkthrough: Poetic Hyperbaton and Dialect

questiontext.text: Why does parsing Homeric epic lines like Iliad 1.1 (Μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος) require human philological expertise?

generalfeedback.text: Poetic hyperbaton and dialectal morphology require human philological expertise to resolve non-projective word order and non-standard inflectional endings.

answer.text: Poetic hyperbaton displaces words from natural word order, while epic dialect features uncontracted vowels, synizesis, and non-Attic genitive endings.

feedback.text: Correct. Epic poetry features non-projective hyperbaton (displaced accusative object) and dialectal morphology (uncontracted -ηος, synizesis in -εω) that break standard Attic parsers.

answer.text: Homeric poetry was composed in modern Latin rather than Ancient Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Homeric epic is composed in an archaic Greek literary dialect fusing Ionic, Aeolic, and Mycenaean elements.

answer.text: Epic poems contain no verbs, requiring all words to be parsed as indeclinable interjections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Epic verse contains fully articulated verbal systems, including root and sigmatic aorists.

answer.text: Automated taggers parse Homeric poetry with 100% precision without needing dictionary lookups.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automated taggers trained on Attic prose suffer high error rates on Homeric dialect forms.

name.text: 22 Question: Encoding Standoff Syntactic Dependencies in TEI XML

questiontext.text: How does TEI XML represent syntactic dependency graphs without disrupting the document's hierarchical tree structure?

generalfeedback.text: TEI and elements represent syntactic dependency graphs by linking head and dependent token IDs without disrupting text hierarchy.

answer.text: By encoding standoff and elements that reference governing head and dependent token @xml:id values.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff linking via and represents complex network graphs independently of XML element nesting hierarchies.

answer.text: By inserting overlapping XML closing tags across sentence boundaries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Overlapping tags violate XML well-formedness rules and cause fatal parse errors.

answer.text: By embedding executable JavaScript scripts directly inside every element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI uses declarative XML linking mechanisms, not embedded scripts, for syntax graphs.

answer.text: By converting all word tokens into external PDF hyperlinks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dependency links connect internal XML token identifiers within the scholarly edition.

name.text: 23 Question: The CoNLL-U Format: The Global Exchange Standard for Syntax Trees

questiontext.text: What are the mandatory ten fields in order for every token line in a standard CoNLL-U file?

generalfeedback.text: CoNLL-U is the 10-column tab-delimited standard used to exchange and evaluate morphological and syntactic treebanks across all modern NLP software.

answer.text: ID, FORM, LEMMA, UPOS, XPOS, FEATS, HEAD, DEPREL, DEPS, and MISC.

feedback.text: Correct. CoNLL-U defines exactly ten tab-delimited columns in fixed sequence: ID, FORM, LEMMA, UPOS, XPOS, FEATS, HEAD, DEPREL, DEPS, and MISC.

answer.text: TOKEN, TRANSLATION, DEFINITION, SYNONYM, ANTONYM, ETYMOLOGY, DATE, AUTHOR, WITNESS, NOTE.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are lexicographical fields; CoNLL-U specifies strict morphosyntactic and dependency fields.

answer.text: XML_ID, TEI_TAG, CSS_CLASS, FONT_SIZE, COLOR, BOLD, ITALIC, UNDERLINE, MARGIN, PADDING.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are CSS/HTML presentation properties, unrelated to CoNLL-U treebank architecture.

answer.text: LINE, STANZA, POEM, BOOK, AUTHOR, METRE, FOOT, CAESURA, SCAN, RHYME.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These describe verse metrics, not Universal Dependencies morphosyntax.

name.text: 24 Question: Inter-Annotator Agreement in Morphosyntactic Annotation

questiontext.text: Why are statistical metrics like Cohen's Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha used to evaluate inter-annotator agreement instead of raw percentage agreement?

generalfeedback.text: Inter-annotator agreement metrics quantify consensus among human annotators, establishing a statistically validated gold standard for machine evaluation.

answer.text: They mathematically account for the probability of chance agreement among annotators, providing an objective measure of consensus.

feedback.text: Correct. Raw percentage agreement overstates consensus on skewed categories; chance-corrected metrics like Kappa calculate true consensus above baseline probability.

answer.text: They automatically correct all grammatical errors made by human annotators without discussion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Agreement metrics evaluate statistical consistency; adjudication meetings resolve disagreements.

answer.text: They measure the typing speed of annotators in words per minute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inter-annotator agreement measures consensus on categorical labels, not data-entry speed.

answer.text: They eliminate the need for having more than one annotator in a project.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Measuring inter-annotator agreement inherently requires multiple independent annotators.

name.text: 25 Question: Edge Cases in Manual Annotation: Clitics, Crasis, and Tmesis

questiontext.text: In Universal Dependencies and CoNLL-U, how should crasis (e.g. Greek κἀγώ from καὶ ἐγώ) and tmesis be handled?

generalfeedback.text: Clitics, crasis, and tmesis require multi-word token segmentation and compound relation tagging to preserve morphological and syntactic integrity.

answer.text: Crasis is split into multi-word token lines with individual sub-token analyses, while tmesis preverbs link to verbs via 'compound:prt'.

feedback.text: Correct. Crasis uses multi-word token spans (e.g. 1-2) with discrete lemma/POS sub-lines; detached tmesis preverbs attach with compound relation labels.

answer.text: Crasis must be deleted from the text and replaced by modern English translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts preserve all attested contractions, decomposing them systematically into sub-tokens.

answer.text: Tmesis preverbs must be merged into single words by deleting all intervening words in the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial manipulation of manuscript word order is unacceptable; tmesis is modeled via dependency relations.

answer.text: Clitics must be permanently capitalized and tagged as proper nouns.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clitics are functional words (pronouns, particles, conjunctions) and are tagged according to their true grammatical function.

name.text: 26 Question: Edge Cases in Manual Annotation: Ellipsis and Null Heads

questiontext.text: How does Universal Dependencies represent nominal sentences with omitted copulas (e.g. Omnia praeclara rara)?

generalfeedback.text: Universal Dependencies handles ellipsis and copula omission by promoting predicate words to clause heads and utilizing the orphan relation for gapped arguments.

answer.text: The predicate adjective (rara) is promoted to the clause head (root), and the subject (Omnia) attaches to it as nsubj.

feedback.text: Correct. In nominal clauses lacking a copula, UD promotes the predicate complement to clause root, attaching the nominal subject directly to it.

answer.text: The sentence is declared invalid and excluded from the treebank.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Copula omission is standard in classical languages and fully supported in UD through predicate promotion.

answer.text: An imaginary phantom token is inserted into the text and assigned a fake manuscript shelfmark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UD avoids inserting ungrounded phantom tokens into primary token sequences in basic treebanks.

answer.text: The first word in the sentence is always designated as root regardless of its part of speech.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dependency heads are determined by grammatical predication, not linear word position.

name.text: 27 Question: Creating the Ground-Truth Benchmark Dataset

questiontext.text: What linguistic criteria must be balanced when selecting a 200–300 word passage for a ground-truth benchmark dataset?

generalfeedback.text: A representative ground-truth dataset spanning regular paradigms, ambiguous forms, and complex syntax is the necessary benchmark for evaluating automated NLP pipelines.

answer.text: It must include regular nominal and verbal paradigms, closed-class particles, instances of morphological ambiguity, and complex syntactic structures.

feedback.text: Correct. A rigorous benchmark must contain a balanced distribution of regular forms, ambiguous homographs, closed-class items, and complex syntax to evaluate NLP pipelines thoroughly.

answer.text: It must consist entirely of third-person singular present indicative regular active verbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A homogeneous dataset fails to test parser resilience on nominal declensions, irregular stems, or complex syntax.

answer.text: It must be written exclusively in modern twentieth-century journalistic prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The benchmark must be selected directly from the historical corpus under study in the course.

answer.text: It must contain only words that begin with the letter alpha.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Passages are selected for representative grammatical and syntactic breadth, not arbitrary orthographic constraints.

name.text: 28 Question: Documenting the Editorial Annotation Schema

questiontext.text: Why must an editorial annotation schema manual accompany a gold-standard linguistic dataset in a version-controlled repository?

generalfeedback.text: A comprehensive annotation manual documents lexical authorities and disambiguation rules, ensuring transparency and reproducibility for the gold-standard dataset.

answer.text: It documents reference lexicographical editions, tokenization rules, taxonomic disambiguation decisions, and dependency attachment conventions for scientific reproducibility.

feedback.text: Correct. An explicit schema manual ensures that editorial decisions and taxonomy interpretations are transparent, allowing other researchers to replicate the dataset.

answer.text: It is required by law to register the text with national copyright offices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotation manuals serve scientific transparency and scholarly reproducibility, not legal copyright registration.

answer.text: It contains the compiler settings used to build the operating system kernel.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The document records linguistic and philological annotation guidelines, not OS kernel parameters.

answer.text: It automatically translates the historical text into five modern languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema manual defines tagging conventions and disambiguation rules, not automated translations.

name.text: 29 Question: Preparing Ground-Truth Data for Automated Testing

questiontext.text: Why must manual annotations be exported and validated in both CoNLL-U and TEI Chapter 18 XML formats before automated scoring?

generalfeedback.text: Exporting manual annotations to validated CoNLL-U and TEI XML files creates the machine-readable evaluation keys required for automated benchmarking.

answer.text: CoNLL-U serves as the standard input/evaluation format for NLP scoring scripts, while TEI XML preserves the annotations within the digital edition repository.

feedback.text: Correct. CoNLL-U is the universal benchmark format for machine evaluation, while TEI Chapter 18 XML embeds the validated linguistic layer into the archival edition.

answer.text: Exporting to two formats allows the editor to delete the underlying manuscript transcriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic transcriptions remain the foundational core of the digital edition.

answer.text: CoNLL-U format is used exclusively for printing physical paper books.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CoNLL-U is a plain-text tab-delimited format engineered specifically for computational NLP pipelines.

answer.text: TEI XML is incompatible with Unicode characters and requires ASCII conversion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML natively requires UTF-8/UTF-16 Unicode character encoding.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Philologist as the Ground Truth

questiontext.text: What fundamental epistemological principle underpins the three-step comparative cycle of Topic 9?

generalfeedback.text: Human philological expertise creates the gold-standard reference against which all deterministic, statistical, and neural models must be measured.

answer.text: Computational algorithms do not establish linguistic truth; they approximate human philological judgment, which remains the definitive gold standard.

feedback.text: Correct. Machine taggers and AI models are probabilistic approximations; expert human philology establishes the ground truth against which all computational tools are measured.

answer.text: Automated neural networks have rendered human philological expertise completely obsolete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Without human ground truth, machine accuracy cannot be evaluated, and models degrade on historical anomalies.

answer.text: Human editors should accept automated parser outputs without checking dictionaries or context.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncritical acceptance of machine output propagates systemic errors throughout digital corpora.

answer.text: Deterministic algorithms and large language models never make morphological or syntactic errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both deterministic and generative models make frequent errors on historical spelling, dialect, and complex syntax.
